examples.problem_statement: It was a fact that the region was both quiet and rural, but what the typically impoverished residents considered (i) _________ refuge was considered by the well-heeled visitors to be an intolerable (ii) _________, and its residents' lifestyles unpleasantly (iii) _________. Blank (i): a parochial / an arcadian / a squalid. Blank (ii): penumbra / utopia / hinterland. Blank (iii): tony / spartan / apollonian.

solution.operation: Mark the clue words "quiet and rural" and note that "refuge" carries positive charge for the residents.
solution.result: Blank (i) needs a positive word about rural life; blanks (ii) and (iii) sit on the visitors' contrasting negative side.
solution.description: Before testing any choice, pull the sentence's own signals: the region is described as quiet and rural, and the residents call it a refuge, which is a positive label. That fixes the charge each blank must carry.

solution.operation: Match blank (i) to the positive-rural requirement: test parochial, arcadian, squalid.
solution.description: Choose the word that conveys a positive view of rural life. Arcadian does exactly that, while the other two options do not carry that favorable rural sense.

solution.operation: Apply the contrast signaled by the visitors' "intolerable" judgment to blank (ii): test penumbra, utopia, hinterland.
solution.description: Fill the second blank with the word that flips the residents' positive view into the visitors' negative one. Hinterland conveys a backwater or undesirable, far-out place, which is the contrast the sentence demands.

solution.operation: Apply the negative requirement carried by "unpleasantly" to blank (iii): test tony, spartan, apollonian.
solution.description: Pick the only choice that can be read as negative in this slot. Of the three offered words, only spartan can carry that negative sense, so it completes the sentence.

key_reminders: A word like "refuge" is itself a charge clue: it tells you the blank beside it must be positive.
When a sentence contrasts two groups' views of the same place, the blanks on opposite sides must take opposite charges.
In a three-blank question, a blank whose choice set offers only one word of the required charge is settled by charge alone.
common_mistakes: Reading "quiet and rural" as inherently negative and choosing parochial or squalid for blank (i), ignoring that the residents call the place a refuge.
Filling blank (ii) with utopia, which repeats the residents' positive view instead of delivering the visitors' "intolerable" verdict.
Treating spartan as merely descriptive and picking tony for blank (iii), which contradicts "unpleasantly".

examples.problem_statement: Select the two answer choices that, when used to complete the sentence, fit the meaning of the sentence as a whole and produce completed sentences that are alike in meaning. The plan, which the engineers said would save the aquifer by reducing pumping to _________ levels, has passed a governmental environmental review but faces opposition from outdoor and environmental groups. Choices: (A) innocuous, (B) feasible, (C) practicable, (D) minimal, (E) remedial, (F) benign.

solution.operation: Read the engineers' claim that the reduced pumping levels would save the aquifer, and ask what kind of levels that implies.
solution.result: The blank must describe levels that do no harm to the aquifer.
solution.description: Start from the sentence's own logic rather than the choices: if the engineers believe the reduced levels will save the aquifer, the blank has to characterize those levels as harmless or curative.

solution.operation: Collect every choice that fits that sense: innocuous, minimal, remedial, benign.
solution.result: A four-word shortlist of contextually acceptable words.
solution.description: Sweep the six options and keep each one an engineer could plausibly use for levels that save the aquifer. Four words survive this contextual filter.

solution.operation: Within the shortlist, look for two words that produce sentences alike in meaning.
solution.result: innocuous and benign pair; minimal and remedial each stand alone.
solution.description: Sentence Equivalence requires a matched pair, not just two workable words. Among the four survivors, only innocuous and benign mean the same thing, so the other two shortlisted words cannot be part of the answer.

solution.operation: Check the remaining near-synonym pair, feasible and practicable, against the context.
solution.result: Rejected: they imply the current levels are not feasible or practicable.
solution.description: Confirm the discarded pair really fails on meaning, not just on charge. These two words are similar to each other, but using them implies the current pumping levels are not feasible, which conflicts with the sentence's implication that the current levels, though perhaps undesirable, are entirely feasible.

examples.answer: Choice A: innocuous AND Choice F: benign

key_reminders: The answer must be a pair of words that are alike in meaning, not merely two words that each fit the blank.
A word can fit the blank's sense and still be wrong if no second choice matches it in meaning.
Rejecting a choice requires showing it distorts what the sentence implies, not just that another choice reads better.
common_mistakes: Selecting feasible and practicable because they form an obvious synonym pair, without testing whether that meaning fits a sentence about saving the aquifer.
Picking minimal and remedial together as though they were synonyms, when each fits the context but neither matches the other in meaning.
Stopping at innocuous alone and treating the question as single-answer rather than finding its benign partner.
